stem: Why did the Homestead Act disappoint many of the settlers it was meant to help, even though the land was free?

stimulus.source_note: Homestead Act of 1862, 12 Stat. 392. Public domain. Text verified against the National Park Service transcription (home.nps.gov/home/homestead-act-of-1862.htm) and Wikisource (en.wikisource.org/wiki/Homestead_Act).
stimulus.text:
Homestead Act of 1862, Sections 1-2 (ellipses mark omissions):

"That any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States, or who shall have filed his declaration of intention to become such, ... shall ... be entitled to enter one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands ... Provided, That any person owning and residing on land may ... enter other land lying contiguous to his or her said land, which shall not, with the land so already owned and occupied, exceed in the aggregate one hundred and sixty acres."

"And upon filing the said affidavit with the register or receiver, and on payment of ten dollars, he or she shall thereupon be permitted to enter the quantity of land specified: Provided, however, That no certificate shall be given or patent issued therefor until the expiration of five years from the date of such entry."

options.text: 160 acres was too small for dry Plains farming, and homes and machinery still cost money
The act gave land only to railroad companies, not to individual farmers
options.misconception: Background: the act gave land to individual settlers; the railroad companies got their land from the Pacific Railway Acts.

options.text: The act required settlers to pay the railroads for the right to ship their crops
options.misconception: Background: freight rates were a real grievance, but they came from the railroads' pricing, not from any clause of the Homestead Act.

options.text: The act forbade settlers from selling their crops in eastern markets
options.misconception: Background: settlers sold wheat and corn into national and international markets; the act placed no ban on selling crops.

rationales.A: Background from the books: 160 acres suited eastern farming, not the dry Plains, and free land still left the settler to pay for a house and expensive machines. Many sold out or failed.
rationales.B: Background: the Homestead Act's claims went to individual settlers. Background: the railroad land grants were a separate law, the Pacific Railway Acts.
rationales.C: Background: high freight rates squeezed farmers, but the charge came from railroad pricing, not from the Homestead Act, which says nothing about shipping.
rationales.D: Background: Plains farmers were drawn into national and international markets. The act never forbade selling crops; the market was the point.
rationales.general:
Free land sounds like a gift until you price what comes with it.
1. Start with the act's own number: 160 acres, fixed for every claim.
2. Add what the books report. Background: that size fit rainy eastern farms, not dry Plains grain and grazing, and houses and machines still cost money.
3. See the result. Background: many settlers could not make the farm pay and sold out, which is why Congress later offered bigger plots.
Remember: free is not the same as workable, so ask what a gift still costs to use.
